claims.text: Rapid quenching creates a kinetic barrier to atomic rearrangement in multi-element, near-equiatomic nanoparticles.
The kinetic barrier hinders elemental diffusion.
Hindered elemental diffusion preserves a high-entropy, near-equiatomic solid solution at service temperatures.
Hindered elemental diffusion prevents phase segregation and intermetallic-compound formation at service temperatures.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles contain a kinetically trapped, metastable high-entropy phase.
The metastable high-entropy phase impedes atomic rearrangements.
Rapid quenching locks in a disordered, chemically homogeneous atomic arrangement.
Slower cooling provides sufficient atomic mobility for phase demixing.
Slower cooling provides sufficient atomic mobility for intermetallic ordering.
After identical high-temperature exposure, rapidly quenched nanoparticles will retain greater compositional homogeneity than slowly cooled nanoparticles.
After identical high-temperature exposure, rapidly quenched nanoparticles will exhibit less elemental segregation than slowly cooled nanoparticles.
After identical high-temperature exposure, slowly cooled nanoparticles will exhibit more phase separation and intermetallic ordering than rapidly quenched nanoparticles.
High mixing entropy is a crucial factor within the proposed applicability domain.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to catalytic service at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric service at 473–1923 K.
